brief: Hand-dyed wool skeins are stacked into a stepped lozenge pyramid, seen straight on. The colours are madder red, indigo, weld yellow, walnut brown and undyed cream. Each twisted hank is rendered hyperreal with dense directional hatching and fine pencil: crimped fibres, stray hairs and slight dye mottling. The arrangement borrows kilim logic, with hard stepped diagonals, saw-tooth edges where skeins meet and strict bilateral balance. There are no curves in the overall form. The light is warm and dry. The piece reads as geometric from afar and woolly up close.

A weathered, lichen-crusted wooden field gate is seen at eye level. A dew-wet cow's nose pushes through the bars, nostrils glistening, with whiskers and pores exact. Behind it, a loosely suggested oak edge and damp meadow dissolve in plein-air haste. Use charcoal mass and broad earthy watercolour washes in raw umber, terre verte, yellow ochre and grey sky. These sharpen into meticulous coloured pencil only at the nose and the grain of the gate. The light is overcast and silvery. The study feels rural and patient, caught outdoors before the weather turns.

A low-horizon sky study: a towering cumulus with a thin cap cloud along its crown. The cap's edge shimmers in pastel diffraction bands of mint, salmon, lilac and pale gold. Paint it in wet-in-wet watercolour with soft blooms for the cloud mass. The spectral fringe is glazed in narrow, carefully blended bands. Below, a sliver of empty carpark tarmac and one sodium lamp post are rendered in precise pen and pencil, anchoring the scale. Most of the picture is luminous sky. The mood is quiet, sudden wonder in a mundane place.

A single speckled brown hen's egg sits in a straw nest at the centre of a Pennsylvania Dutch fraktur sheet. The egg and the straw are rendered with obsessive realism: chalky shell pores, a faint bloom, and individual dried stalks. Around them, flat folk-painted tulips, hearts and paired distelfink birds in vermilion, mustard and verdigris are outlined in brown iron-gall pen. A hand-lettered gothic border frames everything on foxed, laid-texture cream paper. The tension between the naive ornament and the photographic egg drives the picture. It feels devotional, homely and odd.

A bunch of freshly pulled beetroots and carrots, soil still clinging, is arranged like a Zhostovo bouquet on a black lacquer tray. Build it in the tray-painter's sequence: a dim underpainting, then rich transparent watercolour glazes of crimson lake, carrot orange and leaf green. Finish with sharp white highlights on the wet skins and stems. The roots and rootlets are hyperreal. A thin, ornate gold scroll border runs around the tray's rim. The deep black field makes the colour glow. It looks opulent, folkloric and earthy all at once.

A close crop of a woman's face in aviator sunglasses. The lenses reflect a palm-lined coastal road and a red convertible in perfect miniature. Render it hyperreal, but only through flat stacked spot-colour layers like a hand-pulled Cuban film poster: tomato red, ochre, turquoise, cream and dense black. Tones are built by overprinting, not blending, with marker-flat fills and slight misregistration halos. Bold hand-drawn title lettering cuts across the lower third. The edges are hard and the contrast graphic. The feel is cinematic swagger, both handmade and precise.

The upper band shows a striped barber-pole mooring post and a peeling ochre-and-rose plaster wall with green shutters, painted crisply. The larger lower band shows their reflection in a canal. The reflection is fractured into wobbling horizontal ribbons, stretched and broken by small ripples. Render it in layered watercolour, with dragged wet streaks and lifted lights in the water. Fine pen squiggles mark the ripple edges. The palette is ochre, venetian red, bottle green and murky jade. The light is reflective and liquid, making the picture lazy and hypnotic.

Five slices of lotus root are arranged in a perfect radial roundel, the way a Japanese family crest is laid out, and set on a field of glossy black lacquer. Each slice is rendered hyperreal: translucent starchy flesh in pale celadon and ivory, wet sheen around the hollow chambers, and fine root fibres at the rims. A crisp fine-pen contour holds each shape with heraldic discipline. Inside, layered transparent watercolour glazes build the depth. A single thin gold ring encloses the arrangement. The composition is strict and symmetrical. It is emblematic yet edible, like a crest made of real food.

A man's broad back seen from behind, wearing a rumpled rayon aloha shirt soaked through between the shoulder blades. The bold print of hibiscus, monstera and outrigger canoes in coral red, palm green, cream and lagoon teal follows every fold and drape. The fabric is rendered in confident flat watercolour fills, with the print distorting realistically across creases, a sweat-darkened patch and the curve of a shoulder blade. Thin marker outlines crisp the print motifs, and soft shading pools in the folds. The man's sunburnt neck and damp hairline sit at the top edge. The background is a blurred parking lot of pale asphalt, keeping the shirt dominant.

The flank and shoulder of a bay horse, cropped tight, with the coat's hair whorls and growth directions laid out as a vector field. The coat is rendered entirely in long, flowing coloured-pencil strokes that converge into spiral cowlicks and diverge across muscle. A sheen of mahogany, burnt umber, coppery highlight and a cool blue reflected sky runs across the glossy summer coat. Veins, a fly and a dried sweat line under the girth area are drawn with photographic precision. The streamlines must stay readable as pure flow at a distance, and the light is bright midday from above. The ground is a warm ochre paper.

A tumbled heap of sugar cubes beside a demitasse of espresso, painted with photographic fidelity but built entirely from tiny stepped cubes, as if the scene had been sampled into a voxel grid and then lit for real. Every cube shows three flat faces in alcohol-marker tones of bone white, warm grey and cool slate. The crema is built the same way, in stepped tan and burnt umber blocks. The camera is low, at a three-quarter angle across a black lacquer counter. Hard key light from the upper left gives crisp staircase shadows. Edges are knife-clean with no blending, and the realism comes only from correct value relationships.

A living green frog crouched at the rim of a tin-glazed plate. The frog is rendered with hyperreal wet skin, golden iris and pulsing throat, while the plate's surface imitates majolica. A milky opaque white ground carries painted borders of cobalt blue, antimony yellow, copper green and manganese purple. Watercolour pools and crawls where the glaze would have run, with soft blurred edges and tiny pinholes. The frog's own colours echo the glaze palette, so it half belongs to the decoration. Soft diffuse studio light gives a gleaming reflection on the plate's curve. The view is a slightly elevated three-quarter angle, with the plate cropped off two edges.

An extreme close crop of a giraffe's neck curving into its huge long-lashed eye, filling the whole frame edge to edge. The coat's patches are treated explicitly as a Voronoi tessellation: irregular cells of chestnut, liver brown and burnt orange watercolour with pooled wet edges. They are separated by cream channels that thin and widen like true cell boundaries. Over each cell, fine coloured-pencil strokes lay the short hair direction, and the eye is a glossy dark sphere reflecting savanna sky. Warm late-afternoon raking light catches the fur's nap. The pattern is both a mathematical diagram and a living animal.

A car windshield after impact, seen from the driver's seat. A spiderweb of cracks fractures the glass into tilted, splintered planes, and each shard reflects a slightly different sky, overpass girder or dashboard fragment. The planes are rendered in sharp graphite with ruled ink edges. Some are filled with cool cerulean watercolour, some with sodium yellow and some left raw paper. Perspective deliberately disagrees between shards, like a deconstructivist facade collapsing inward. Laminated glass shows its milky refraction lines at the impact point. There is no central subject, only angular tension and diagonals running off every edge. A tiny air-freshener tree hangs perfectly crisp in the foreground.

The interior of a craft brewery: a gleaming copper mash tun, riveted seams and a tangle of stainless pipes, valves and pressure gauges. Everything is painted with Precisionist hard edges and no human presence. Flat, ruled watercolour planes in polished copper, burnt sienna, gunmetal blue-grey and clean ivory wall meet at razor pen lines. Reflections are simplified into crisp geometric bands, yet rivet heads, condensation beads and brushed-steel grain are rendered with total photographic accuracy. Cool, even north light comes through a high clerestory. The composition stacks verticals and pipe diagonals into a near-abstract machine cathedral, cropped tight at the top.

An elderly man in a quilted coat sits on a concrete bench under a swooping cantilevered bus shelter on an empty steppe road. Behind him, a vast mosaic of a stylised cosmonaut fills the shelter's back wall, with chipped tesserae in smalt blue, brick red and ochre. Raw concrete is built in layered charcoal with board-form grain and rust bleeding from rebar. The mosaic is laid in small square watercolour dabs separated by grey grout lines. Overcast flat light gives no hard shadows, and the palette is cold and chalky. The man is placed off-centre to the right, dwarfed by the architecture. His stubble and watery eyes are rendered with uncomfortable photographic precision.

A rock tide pool seen straight down from above. Anemones, a hermit crab, limpets and kelp are rendered in hyperreal detail beneath slightly rippled water, but the pool is mapped like a nautical chart. Fine sepia pen contour lines trace the depths. Pale buff watercolour marks the dry rock, graded aqua and cerulean washes mark the shallows and deeper water, and dotted danger-rock symbols sit beside actual barnacles. A faint compass rose is etched into the stone at one corner. The light is high and clean, with caustic light networks shimmering on the pool floor. The surface is an aged chart paper tone.

A barn owl's face stares frontally, filling the frame, assembled like marquetry. The heart-shaped disc, eyes, beak and speckled breast are each a separate veneer shape: sycamore cream, walnut, rosewood, satinwood and ebony. Each piece carries its own pencil-hatched wood grain running in a deliberately chosen direction. Hot-sand scorch shading darkens the edges of pieces to model the form. Thin knife-cut seams separate the shapes. From a distance the feathers read as photographic, but up close they are pure joinery. The palette is warm and honeyed.

A tightrope walker's foot in a worn leather slipper, gripping a frayed steel cable. It is rendered with obsessive hyperrealism: scuffs, darned stitches, chalk dust and the cable's twisted strands. The foot is set inside the loud graphics of a vintage circus poster. Radiating sunburst bands of crimson, mustard yellow and royal blue fill the ground in flat marker. A coarse spray halftone fades the bands toward the edges, and a star-studded border frames a deep sky drop beneath the wire. The composition is a dramatic upward diagonal with the wire slashing corner to corner. Harsh spotlight from below casts the slipper in theatrical glare.

A halved lemon resting on the blade of an old carbon-steel knife, rendered entirely in engraver's line like a bond certificate vignette. Swelling and tapering parallel lines model the pith, the pulp segments and every glistening juice sac. Dense crosshatch carves the shadow, and dot-and-lozenge stipple builds the pitted rind. The only ink is deep banknote green on cream laid paper. Around the subject runs a faint geometric lathe-work border that never quite closes, with the lemon breaking through its frame. Light is crisp and frontal. The realism must be painstaking: knife patina, a seed caught on the edge, a drop about to fall, all achieved through line weight alone.
